extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners before the USPTO; respondents and counsel in USPTO disciplinary proceedings; OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory and procedural standards applied in USPTO disciplinary cases: rules on answering complaints, definitions of professional misconduct, investigatory cooperation, and the four-factor sanction analysis (including exclusion from practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer — admission/default (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in a default judgment." (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not timely answer a disciplinary complaint, the allegations may be deemed admitted and the USPTO may obtain a default judgment. The decision treats such deemed admissions as the basis for factual findings when no answer or response is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response deadline — 30 days after complaint mailed
rubrics_metrics.description: A response (answer) to a Complaint is due 30 days after the Complaint is mailed, not when it is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is measured from the mailing date. Late receipt does not extend the deadline; respondents must track the mailing date to compute the deadline. In this case the answer was due on or before Nov 14, 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction of Administrative Law Judges (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative Law Judges are authorized to hear USPTO disciplinary proceedings and to issue initial decisions under the cited regulations and applicable interagency agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural authority: ALJs (including those via interagency agreement) may adjudicate OED complaints and enter decisions including default judgments and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct — disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misappropriation of client or firm funds is characterized as disreputable or gross misconduct supporting disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not '[e]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate diversion of client or firm funds for personal use qualifies as conduct involving dishonesty and supports a finding of professional misconduct under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension or disbarment as misconduct evidence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that constitutes a violation of §§ 10.23(a) and (b) includes '[s]uspension or disbarment from practice as an attorney or agent on ethical grounds by any duly constituted authority of a State or the United States.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior suspension or disbarment by a state court or other authority may itself be a basis for finding misconduct under the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation/aiding violation of USPTO Rules — professional misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to '[v]iolate or attempt to violate the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, knowingly assist or induce another to do so, or do so through the acts of another.' (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts that violate USPTO professional rules or assisting others to do so are independently sanctionable; this supports discipline beyond state-bar actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose or cooperate in disciplinary/reinstatement matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner in connection with a disciplinary or reinstatement matter shall not 'fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known by the person to have arisen in the matter, fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admission disciplinary authority....' (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-response to lawful investigatory requests (e.g., RFIs) and failure to correct misapprehensions are professional misconduct; cooperation with OED investigations is mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to '[e]ngage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.' (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal to cooperate with investigations or deceitful conduct that undermines trust in the legal system supports a finding under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond to OED Requests for Information (RFIs) constitutes misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal or failure to answer RFIs sent by the Office of Enrollment and Discipline is a failure to cooperate and a violation of USPTO professional conduct provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Respondent did not respond to RFIs dated Dec 28, 2012 and May 22, 2013; the decision treats this refusal as violating § 11.801(b) and related misconduct provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 1 — Violation of a duty (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the practitioner violate a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession? (One of the four factors for sanction consideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of fiduciary duties (e.g., diverting client/escrow funds without consent) strongly support severe sanctions, including maximum penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 2 — State of mind (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the practitioner act intentionally, knowingly, or negligently? (Second factor under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, knowing, or intentional misconduct (especially long-term, intentional theft) favors maximum sanctions; negligence may warrant milder sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 3 — Amount of actual or potential injury (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: What amount of actual or potential injury was caused by the practitioner's misconduct? (Third factor under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial actual or potential financial harm to clients or firms supports harsher sanctions. Example: actual loss within limitations was $23,000 but potential/total diversion was at least $96,000, supporting maximum sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 4 — Aggravating and mitigating factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any aggravating or mitigating factors? (Fourth factor under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors include selfish motive, pattern/length of misconduct, experience/knowledge of wrongdoing, and lack of cooperation. Mitigating factors can include lack of prior disciplinary record and partial repayment/settlement. The presence of significant aggravators can outweigh mitigators and support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deemed admissions as basis for factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a respondent fails to answer, the respondent is 'deemed to have admitted each of the factual allegations' in the complaint and the court may base findings on those admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When admissions are deemed, the court may treat the complaint's factual allegations as established facts without further proof; this is the procedural consequence of default under § 11.36(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from practice before the USPTO as available sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may request, and the Court may order, exclusion of a practitioner from practice before the USPTO (in patent, trademark, or other matters) as a disciplinary sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is appropriate when the sanction factors (duty violated, state of mind, injury, aggravators/mitigators) support such a penalty. In this case, on the basis of deemed admissions and factor analysis, the Court ordered exclusion.
